entries.title: Massie and Khanna Have Enough Signatures for a Second Epstein Files Discharge Petition
entries.summary: The chamber, however, won’t be able to vote on the bill until after November’s midterm elections.
entries.content:
Reps. Thomas Massie and Ro Khanna announced Thursday that they have amassed enough signatures to bring a vote on a second bill to force the release of files related to the disgraced financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Four Republicans, including Massie, of Kentucky, Reps. Ralph Norman and Nancy Mace, both of South Carolina, and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, have agreed to sign on to a discharge petition for a measure dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act II — joining every Democrat, Massie said in a social media post.

The chamber, however, won’t be able to vote on the bill until after November’s midterm elections. House Speaker Mike Johnson and Republican leadership cut the legislative session short by one day this week, just days after Massie proposed a privileged resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Under House rules, the measure would have come up for a vote by Thursday had the House’s workweek not been cut short.

“Thomas Massie and I have defied history a second time, securing commitments for 218 signatures on Epstein 2.0,” Khanna, a California Democrat, wrote on X. “Two Democrats were sick and will sign the day Johnson calls us back in.”

In July, Massie and Khanna introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II — named after another bill passed last year which mandated the release of millions of documents pertaining to the Epstein case. The new bill gives victims, lawmakers and states the power to sue the Justice Department for unlawfully concealing Epstein-related files.

That bill has since stalled in committee, but a discharge petition with 218 signatures will allow Massie and Khanna to bring it directly to the floor for a vote without the approval of House leadership.

That same number of votes — a simple majority — is all that’s needed to send the bill to the Senate.

“We will not rest until the Epstein abusers are held accountable and there is justice,” Khanna said.

The House passed the first Epstein Files Transparency Act in a stunning, near-unanimous November vote, following months of resistance from Republicans and President Donald Trump.

The DOJ has since produced millions of documents, emails and financial records related to the Epstein case, though the release was met with widespread accusations of a government cover-up, concerns about botched redactions and political fights over omitted records. Massie and Khanna maintain the department has “grossly failed” to meet legal requirements.

Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Justice Department are also the targets of a lawsuit filed by Katie Phang, a lawyer and political commentator, to force the release of additional files related to Epstein. On Wednesday, a federal judge warned Blanche that he could be held in contempt if he failed to comply with court orders to produce unreleased FBI interview notes and foreign-language materials that were omitted from the department’s initial release.

A spokesperson for the DOJ brushed off the warning in a Thursday statement to The Washington Sun, saying that department leadership “is not ‘concerned’ about this case, and our filings will speak for themselves.”
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: USPS Chief Says Work Has Stopped on Trump’s Voter Eligibility Database
entries.summary: “There’s an injunction so we’re not doing anything,” postmaster general David Steiner told The Associated Press in an interview.
entries.content:
By Steven Sloan

The top official at the U.S. Postal Service said Thursday that the agency has stopped work on developing a controversial computer system that was central to President Donald Trump’s effort to limit mail voting after the Supreme Court rejected his executive order this week.

“There’s an injunction so we’re not doing anything,” postmaster general David Steiner told The Associated Press in an interview.

Steiner, a onetime chief executive of Waste Management, has spent most of the past year atop the postal service navigating political and financial challenges. He’s pressing Congress for changes that would help him resolve what he has called a “liquidity crisis.”

And Trump’s efforts to largely eradicate mail voting turned the postal service into an unlikely arbiter of who is eligible to vote just months before this year’s critical midterm elections, a role Steiner seemingly had little interest in playing. Unlike Trump, who was sharply critical of the Supreme Court decision and ridiculed some of the justices, Steiner offered no assessment of the court’s action.

Steiner also declined to take a position on Trump’s policy, presenting himself as the leader of an “independent agency of the executive branch” whose influence over the president’s order was limited to operational concerns.

“I don’t get to decide what rules that are put on us that I decide to accept or not accept,” he said. “I looked at it more from the execution side.”

The postal service has asserted its independence in the past, including during a 2019 standoff when the first Trump administration sought to pressure the agency as the president was in a dispute with Amazon. Steiner said he wouldn’t get into the “nuance” of that.

But the pressure has grown so intense at points that it’s fueled talk of whether Steiner might resign, a notion he denied.

“There’s no truth to that,” he said. “I think I know the motivation behind it. I think it’s somebody that would like to see me out of a job.”

Inserting the Postal Service into elections

The executive order Trump signed in March directed several federal agencies to develop state citizenship lists. Those lists would have been delivered to an online portal at the Postal Service, which would have been allowed to send mail ballots only to voters who were cleared through the process. Steiner said he knew about the order about a month before it was unveiled but said his focus was largely on implementation, not the policy’s merits.

A whistleblower report released earlier this month by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., argued the system was hastily built and riddled with errors.

Steiner said he read “portions” of the whistleblower report and acknowledged the obstacles associated with building such a massive platform quickly. Still, he said he had confidence in colleagues working on the project and had planned to unveil it around Sept. 15.

“There’s absolutely no doubt that we worked fast,” he said. “My personal opinion is it was a monumental task and I’m very proud of our IT department for being able to do it that fast.”

In addition to the voter list, Trump’s order would have required states to adopt a uniform envelope style that included barcodes, something states said would have been arduous so close to the election.

Following the Supreme Court’s ruling, a memo sent to all postal service employees Wednesday and obtained by the AP said the agency will “not be enforcing any of these new rules in the 2026 federal election.”

“First and foremost, for Election Mail it is business as usual,” according to the memo. “We continue to follow established protocols, and we remain entirely focused on our core mission: delivering the mail safely and securely for voters and election officials across the country.”

Though the Supreme Court rejected Trump’s executive order for this year’s election, Justice Brett Kavanaugh indicated he might rule in favor of the administration if the issue comes back before the court at a later time.

Steiner encourages voters to cast ballots early

Steiner said the postal service would still encourage the use of envelopes and barcodes in future elections, which it has long recommended. He said such changes wouldn’t be required but those who don’t comply may have to pay more.

“If you use the barcode in the envelope, we’ll charge you a lower price,” he said. “If you don’t, we’re going to charge you a higher price because it’s harder for us to process.”

While the postal service isn’t moving forward on Trump’s order, there are still concerns about postmark delays that could have an impact on this year’s elections. The number of ballots rejected for late postmarks has soared in the vote-by-mail states of Washington and Oregon, according to recently released data highlighting concerns about recent changes in postal service operations.

Steiner said there were no plans to alter those operations and encouraged voters who use mail to get their ballots in early.

“We say seven days,” he said. “Everything is solved if people vote early.”
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Maryland Police Charge a Man in Connection to Missing Child’s Death 33 Years Later
entries.summary: Investigators recently reopened George Burdynski Jr.’s long-cold case.
entries.content:
Authorities in Prince George’s County arrested a man Wednesday in connection with the disappearance of 10-year-old George Burdynski Jr., a Maryland resident who went missing 33 years ago.

Burdynski was last seen May 24, 1993, biking away from his family’s home in Brentwood. County police later uncovered a child-sex-abuse ring near Burdynski’s residence in their initial investigation into his disappearance, but none of the three men convicted for those crimes were officially connected to Burdynski’s case, which remained unsolved.

County Police Chief George Nader said in a Thursday news conference that investigators who were reevaluating the cold case in the past few months spoke with a currently unnamed 46-year-old man who admitted to killing Burdynski after facing yearslong abuse from Joseph Lynch, who lived near the victim and was among those convicted after the child-sex-abuse-ring arrests.

Authorities allege Lynch sexually abused Burdynski, as well as the 46-year-old man when he was 13, before he had the then-13-year-old boy sexually abuse and murder Burdynski and dispose of his body in a dumpster.

At the start of the news conference, Burdynski’s sister Virginia shared how the news felt to their family.

“First, I would like to say, Junior, I’m so sorry for what happened to you,” Virginia said, close to tears. “I’m so sorry for what you had to go through. We’ve held on to hope for 33 years. This is not what we prayed for. This is incredibly devastating. Our hearts are shattered. We love you, Junior.”

Due to the amount of time since the incident, Nader said recovery of Burdynski’s body is unlikely, and did not comment on how much other physical evidence authorities have that could point to Lynch’s involvement, as the investigation is still active.

Lynch faces a second-degree-murder charge in relation to the death of Burdynski as well as “associated charges,” Nader said. State’s Attorney Tara Jackson said Lynch’s bond hearing is expected to be held in district court on Friday or Monday.

These new charges come after authorities charged Lynch earlier this year with sexually abusing two teenage boys multiple times from 2007 to 2014 in Mount Rainier. He is currently in custody in connection with those assaults and a 2012 arson.

The 46-year-old man has not been charged in relation to Burdynski’s death.

“We’ve been working with the detectives to help them bring charges in this case, and we will continue to evaluate, but the charges are what they are,” Jackson said.

Nader capped the news conference by asking anyone with information about the case, or anyone who believes they may have been a victim of Lynch’s, to contact the Prince George's County Police Department.

“I absolutely believe there are other victims associated with this case,” he said.

entries.title: DOJ Officials Brush Off a Judge’s Contempt Warning in the Epstein Files Case
entries.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche has until Sept. 24 to produce the unreleased documents and redacted names to the court.
entries.content:
After a federal judge again told Attorney General Todd Blanche that the Justice Department could face civil contempt charges if it continues to refuse court orders to produce a tranche of new Epstein documents, a department spokesperson said leadership is not “concerned” about the warnings.

In a Wednesday order, U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan gave Blanche until next Thursday to produce records for the Washington, D.C., court — or explain by the Monday before why the task is too unclear to complete. Sullivan alluded to potential contempt charges if Blanche fails to comply.

In response to questions from The Washington Sun about Sullivan’s warning, a department spokesperson said leadership “is not ‘concerned’ about this case, and our filings will speak for themselves.”

The DOJ has refused to answer whether Blanche will comply with Sullivan’s orders to produce the documents in question: a set of specific FBI interview notes and unreleased foreign-language documents requested by Katie Phang, a lawyer and political broadcaster with close ties to some of Epstein’s victims. The department must also provide documentation supporting its redactions in a series of emails.

The DOJ has released millions of records mandated by the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which was passed by Congress last year. Phang contends that some of the names redacted in those volumes may belong to conspirators of the now-deceased human trafficker.

Blanche already missed a June deadline to produce the records, and Sullivan rejected many of his team’s attempts to justify why certain documents should be exempt from public view. At an August hearing, Sullivan warned government lawyers that contempt proceedings could ruin their careers.

“The public has a right to know what the hell is going on,” he said.

The department continued to maintain as it has in previous court filings that it has already met the court’s standards in its statement to The Sun on Thursday.

“We have already shown the Judge ‘proof of redacted victim names’ and established that the plaintiff in this case seeks to unmask victim names,” the spokesperson said.

Phang is suing for the production of the Epstein files, redacted legally and with lawful withholdings, not this “slaphappy bullshit that we’ve received from Todd Blanche,” she said in a video on her Meidas Touch show Thursday.

“Blanche should have done it back in June,” Phang said. “He’s lucky he didn’t already get his ass defaulted by Judge Sullivan. But now that he’s going to be forced to answer the complaint, the bigger case — the big push for all of the documents — can move forward.”

The DOJ filed a notice Thursday asking the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals to review Sullivan’s injunction.
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Inside House Democrats' Push to Kick Old People Out of Leadership
entries.summary: Some newer members say they don’t want to wait decades before they get to lead major committees.
entries.content:
Insurgent House Democrats are opening a new front in the generational war roiling the party, pushing to put term limits on committee leadership roles.

When the lawmakers return to Washington after the midterms, some Democrats plan to bring up a proposal in their caucus organizational meetings that would limit how many years leaders remain in top committee stops, according to multiple House Democrats familiar with the plans.

“It will only happen if members approve it. It’s an uphill battle, but I think the tide is turning,” said one of the House Democrats who was granted anonymity to address internal deliberations. “We are working on it. It’s a very touchy topic.”

A second House Democrat said that next Congress, “there’ll be many more members that are five terms or less” and there is an “appetite” to add limits so that younger and newer members can move up.

The new discussion around term limits comes at a time when the Democratic base is calling for new faces in the party and multiple incumbents have lost primaries to younger, more progressive candidates. Already, Democrats are starting to mount challenges for top committee slots: Rep. Jahana Hayes of Connecticut announced she’d challenge Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia for the top job on the House Education and Workforce Committee. Scott ascended to that position in 2015.

Unlike Democrats, Republicans impose a strict six-year limit on lawmakers serving as chairs or as ranking members when their party is in the minority. The first House Democrat said the limits could be similar to Republicans’ but without counting the years as ranking members, though the details on the restrictions are still being worked through. The lawmaker also said that an additional proposal is to allow committee leaders who have reached their limit to request a waiver.

Rep. Mike Levin of California, the chair of the House Democratic Committee on Caucus Rules, said the panel has held multiple listening sessions where the seniority issue came up.

“There are a number of members that obviously have great interest in this. There’s been discussion of grandfathering in everybody who’s already in a ranking member or chair position,” Levin said. “There’s others that disagree with that, so there’s been no consensus on that, nor has there been any finalized proposal or anything like that. We’re still working on it.”

Levin said that the committee would work with members who are interested in the rule change to “formulate specific proposals that will be voted on.” Once there is a proposal, it will be voted on by the entire caucus rules committee, and then brought to the full House Democratic caucus for a vote in November.

“My hope is that we can build some internal consensus on what would be fair, or I should say, not just what would be fair, but what would actually earn the support of our members,” Levin added.

The issue is especially touchy for Congressional Black Caucus members who have historically supported seniority rules. Those rules have helped secure top slots for Black members who were long denied power in Congress. And the proposal comes as fewer Black lawmakers are expected in the next Congress because of Republicans’ redistricting efforts, potentially reducing the caucus’ influence.

Maryland Rep. Glenn Ivey told The Washington Sun that a proposal for term limits is a “mixed bag,” pointing at the House GOP’s practices.

“Watching what the Republicans are doing, they’re just playing musical chairs sometimes with these committee chairmanships to sort of circumvent what the goal is,” Ivey said. “On the Democratic side, we’ve had very young members — Robert Garcia for example — rise to the top.”

Three Democrats pointed to Rep. Frank Pallone (D-New Jersey), who has been the top Democrat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since 2015, as one of the biggest opponents to term limits.

“Over the years, he’s been very adamant that he is against it. Very, very adamant, and talks to all the members saying, ‘Don’t be for it,’” a third House Democrat told The Sun. “He feels like he’s waited a long time to get there and he doesn’t want it to change.”

In a statement to The Sun, Pallone said, “our current system is democracy — every two years, members have the freedom to run and vote for the best person to lead committees based on merit. Open campaigns lead to healthy debate, diverse leaders, and a stronger caucus.”

Other senior Democrats are also likely to challenge the term limits efforts in November.

Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin, a popular House Democrat who has been the top Democrat of two powerful committees — first the Oversight Committee and now Judiciary — called himself “a pretty good example of why we don’t need term limits, because we do have real and open elections on the Democratic side.”

“There are people who may want to run for a chairmanship who feel like there's too much of a presumption of seniority, and it’s only a presumption, it’s a rebuttable presumption,” Raskin added. “I can see where it's coming from, but we've also seen a lot of turnover and fluidity in the ranking positions and the chair positions.”

Yet, Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson, who has been the top Democrat in the House Homeland Security Committee since its inception in 2005, told The Sun, “I got to be chair based on my seniority on the committee.”

“If you ask Bennie Thompson, I support seniority and the current rule. But I will say if you want to debate it and put it to a vote, officer. Fine. That doesn't mean I'll change my vote,” Thompson added.

Some of the lawmakers in line to become chairs if Democrats win the majority in November, such as Garcia, a younger member from California, are not opposed to limits.

“I’ve told folks already in the caucus that I could support that,” said Garcia, who is in line to chair the House Oversight Committee. “I’ve told folks already in the caucus that I could support that.”

“As a new person, I think that having new leaders and there being a debate on that is healthy,” Garcia added.

Previous attempts by Democrats to place term limits on committee chairs have failed. Illinois Rep. Bill Foster led an effort in 2022 to set a six-year limit for committee leaders, counting time served as chair and ranking member together. House Democrats rejected the proposal in a 138-63 vote.

The fact that the proposal got support from around a third of the caucus signaled that such an effort would “eventually” succeed, the third anonymous House Democrat told The Sun.

“A lot of the younger members don’t want to be in Congress for 30 years before they get a chance to chair a major committee. My guess is that if it doesn’t change this time, it’s definitely changing the next time,” the lawmaker said. “It’s just a matter of time. People are watching their Republican classmates come in and have opportunity to chair major committees and leave instead of having to be here for a long time.”

Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee,opposes committee leadership term limits and told The Sun that House Democrats have “created many opportunities” for younger members to move up.

Under the current House Democratic caucus rules, each committee must have a vice chair or vice ranking member position that goes to a member who has served in the committee for five terms or less and is considered “an opportunity for a junior Member to gain insight and experience into the workings of the committee.”

“Contrary to some belief, it does take a little bit of time to understand how this place functions,” Meeks said. “I sat and I watched and I learned for a long period of time.”

But not all Democrats want to wait long to rise through the ranks.

“A lot of us don’t want to stay here forever,” the third House Democrat said.
entries.author: Oriana González, Stephen Neukam

entries.title: Metro Yellow Line Will Be Shut Down for Next Two Weekends
entries.summary: There are also plans to use a single track for the Yellow and Blue lines next week, and to single-track the Red Line in early October.
entries.content:
The Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority is shutting down the Metro’s Yellow Line the next two weekends to work on the route’s rail infrastructure as part of WMATA’s new infrastructure program.

The Yellow Line, which typically runs trains every six minutes on weekdays and every nine minutes on weekends, travels north to south through the District, with stops from Huntington through L’Enfant Plaza to Greenbelt.

Shuttering the Yellow Line comes as the WMATA transitions to a new program that involves crews working overnight and on weekends to tackle preventive repairs, according to the Metro website.

The WMATA also plans to use a single track for the Yellow and Blue lines between 9:30 a.m. and 3 p.m. on Sept. 23, from Reagan National Airport to Pentagon City, to de-stress the rails and prevent heat kinks.

Metro workers are scheduled to single-track the Red Line from Oct. 3 to 4, between Farragut North and Judiciary Square, to fasten the route’s rail, replace its insulator and rehabilitate the line’s grout pad.

During that same time, the WMATA will also single-track the Silver Line from East Falls Church to McLean to replace the line’s switch timber ties, insulators and fasteners.

From Dec. 16 to 30, crews will single-track the Green Line between U Street and Georgia Avenue-Petworth to replace its rail and fastening systems; communications and signal equipment; and lighting infrastructure.

The WMATA says it may change the scheduled maintenance due to weather, construction delays and other factors outside its control.
entries.author: Justice Covert

entries.title: Hegseth’s Preferred Army Chief Faces Long Odds in the Senate
entries.summary: Republican lawmakers say Sean Parnell’s abuse allegations and restrictions on the Pentagon press are liabilities to getting confirmation votes.
entries.content:
Republican senators said they see no path to confirmation for Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, as a potential Army secretary, complicating the prospects for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s preferred candidate as the White House considers a wider field.

The reluctance underscores the liabilities Parnell would bring to a confirmation fight, including abuse allegations he has denied and his role implementing Hegseth’s restrictions on the Pentagon press corps. Several less controversial candidates are also in the mix as the White House weighs who should lead the Army through an ongoing war with Iran, strained arms stockpiles and an ambitious modernization push.

Parnell emerged as Hegseth’s favored candidate last month to succeed Dan Driscoll, who resigned after months of tension with Hegseth over the defense secretary’s removal of senior officers. But Parnell is already encountering pushback from Republicans whose confirmation votes he would need.“It’s hard for me to imagine that could possibly happen,” Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said when asked about the prospect of Parnell making it through the Senate. “His record, particularly the spousal abuse stuff, is just a bridge too far for the vast majority of people. Not to mention there are other good people.”

A Senate Republican aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter, took a similar view about Parnell’s prospects. “It’s just simply not feasible,” the aide said. “Everyone knows the backing just isn’t there.”

Parnell has denied the abuse allegations, which his estranged wife made during divorce and child-custody proceedings and that surfaced during Parnell's aborted run for Senate in 2021.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said he would vote against Parnell if President Donald Trump nominates him, arguing he lacks independence and experience.

“I feel like we need less of an echo chamber” at the Pentagon, said Tillis, who is retiring after his second term ends in January. “If we’re going to have to have Hegseth in this role, I’d at least like to have more people around him that are going to be more independent and look around corners. I don’t see Parnell doing that.”

Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth, has since become one of the secretary’s most outspoken Republican critics. He also faulted Parnell for implementing Hegseth’s ouster of the Pentagon’s resident press corps.

“That's already demonstrated a lack of confidence,” Tillis said. “If you're proud of your work product, you want press to ask you the tough questions and answer them. If you're worried about it, then you box them out.”

The White House has not named Driscoll’s successor, but two people familiar with the deliberations describe a broader White House vetting process. It’s being overseen by the White House, the people familiar said, and the ability to get a nominee through the Senate is a priority.

In response to a request for comment, the Pentagon repeated its recent statement, saying that Parnell is “100%” focused on his current job. The White House said Trump would make a choice on his own timetable.

“The President will announce a nominee for the next Secretary of the Army at a time and place of his choosing — statements from anonymous sources claiming to have insight into the President’s thinking should be treated as mere speculation,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement.

Kelly also praised Driscoll’s tenure, saying he had advanced Trump’s agenda by emphasizing readiness and lethality, and assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine.

One U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter, defended Parnell’s record and said Hegseth has personally made the case for him to Trump. Hegseth has also discussed Parnell with White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino in recent weeks, according to the official.

A separate person familiar with the matter said that Parnell was among multiple names Hegseth presented to the Presidential Personnel Office, which acts as an executive search firm.

The U.S. official said Parnell is an excellent candidate to lead the Army, pointing to his combat experience and his 18 months working inside the Pentagon, arguing Parnell knows how to navigate the department’s bureaucracy and has relationships needed to carry out Trump and Hegseth’s agenda.

“He knows how the building operates; he knows the ins and outs,” the official said. “He knows who to talk to and how to get things done.”

The abuse allegations are a non-issue, the official said, noting that the judge who initially awarded full custody to his wife vacated that order and that Parnell and his former wife now share custody of their children.

Parnell has some Republican support. Sen. Dave McCormick, from Parnell’s home state of Pennsylvania, said Thursday on social media that he hoped Parnell was being considered for the role and praised Parnell’s “great family.”“Sean is a good friend, a decorated combat veteran, a true patriot, and a fellow Pennsylvanian,” McCormick said. “I have full confidence that if Sean is given the honor of serving in this role, he will do so with courage and distinction.”Several other Republican senators this week praised Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, a longtime Senate aide who was the Senate-confirmed assistant secretary for civil works when Trump elevated him to the acting role earlier this month. “I like that guy who’s in there, Adam Telle,” said Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama), a senior Senate Armed Services Committee member. “He’d be pretty hard to beat. He’s doing a great job.”Cramer said he would be “very happy” with Telle and said the acting secretary has one significant advantage over other potential candidates: senators already know him.“Adam is so solid,” Cramer said. “He talks with them so respectfully, and they respond in kind, even when they disagree.”Beyond his Senate ties, Telle has strong relationships with the White House and Hegseth, which could ease his path to confirmation if he were nominated.

He served for four years as chief of staff to Sen. Bill Hagerty (R-Tennessee) and previously worked for then-Sens. Thad Cochran and Richard Shelby and on the Senate Appropriations Committee. During Trump’s first term, Telle worked in the White House Office of Legislative Affairs, where his responsibilities included national security and appropriations.

Telle played a substantial role in preparing Hegseth for his confirmation, helping to organize mock hearings and facilitating Hegseth’s meetings with senators.

Other candidates for the Army secretary job include Dane Hughes, the assistant secretary for legislative affairs, and Army Comptroller Marc Andersen — who has been reaching out to lawmakers to make his case for the job, according to one of the people familiar with the deliberations. Derrick Anderson, the Pentagon’s assistant secretary for special operations and low-intensity conflict, and Mike Obadal, the Army under secretary, are also possible candidates.

Democrats are unlikely to provide votes to confirm Trump’s pick for Driscoll’s successor because of broader tensions about Hegseth and the Trump administration’s national security policies. That leaves Senate Republicans with little wiggle room to lose any votes in the confirmation process, and that threshold appears to be breached with several Republicans saying Parnell is a no-go for them.Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona), an Armed Services member who voted for some of Trump’s nominees this term, said he now regrets some of those votes because administration officials have failed to show enough independence from the president. “I admit when I make mistakes,” Kelly said. “Some of these people seemed competent and could be their own person. Almost every one of them turned into a yes-person for Donald Trump, and they will not speak truth to power.”
entries.author: Joe Gould

entries.title: Warren Buffett Steps Down as Berkshire Hathaway Chairman
entries.summary: His son will become replace him.
entries.content:
By Michelle Chapman

Warren Buffett is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway after serving in the role for more than 50 years.

Buffett, 96, will become chairman emeritus and will take on his new role immediately, the company said Friday. His son, Howard, will become Berkshire Hathaway’s new chairman. Howard Buffett has been on the Berkshire Hathaway board since 1993.

Warren Buffett will remain a director. He had served as Berkshire Hathaway’s chairman since 1970.

Buffett stepped down as CEO of the company late last year. He was succeeded by Greg Abel.

“I have served Berkshire since 1965," Buffett said in a letter to shareholders. “Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world. That is not something many people my age can say, and I have never felt better about what comes next.”

Buffett said that he is confident with Abel and his son Howard leading Berkshire Hathaway.

“Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet,” he said. “Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against.”

Buffett's fortune has been amassed through Berkshire Hathaway stock. It was worth more than $140 billion in July 2026.

He has already given away roughly $66 billion worth of stock since 2006.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Mystics 110, Sky 80: Game Recap
entries.summary: Shakira Austin broke Washington’s single-season scoring record in the game.
entries.content:
CHICAGO (AP) — Shakira Austin scored 20 points, Kiki Iriafen finished with 18 points and 11 rebounds, and the Washington Mystics beat the Chicago Sky 110-80 on Thursday night in their first game since the FIBA World Cup break.

The Mystics (25-16), tied with Dallas for sixth in the WNBA standings, moved a half-game ahead of New York. The top four have home court advantage in the best-of-three first round of the playoffs, which begin Sept. 27.

Courtney Vandersloot led Chicago with 14 points and Sydney Taylor scored 12. Kamilla Cardoso and Gabriela Jaquez each added 10 points.

Iriafen, who had her 21st double-double this season, grabbed four offensive rebounds to set a franchise single-season record with 115.

Austin made a layup in the opening minute to break Washington’s single-season scoring record. The 6-foot-5 center went into the game with 657 points this season, which tied the previous mark set by Sonia Citron in 2025.

Georgia Amoore and Michaela Onyenwere added 12 points apiece and Cotie McMahon scored 11 for the Mystics. Citron (personal reasons) did not play.

The Sky (15-26) have lost four in a row following a season-high three consecutive wins.

DiJonai Carrington (foot) did not play for Chicago.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: ‘Safe and Beautiful’
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 18, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: A federal show of force, Bowser’s legacy and the Goodman League.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit: 6/10. Humidity may be slow to drop, but at least we’re headed the right direction. A warm day with a mix of clouds and sun, plus only an isolated shower. Read the full forecast.







THE LATEST

A federal surge into a D.C. neighborhood has left some parents on edge.

Students, staff and parents at Bruce-Monroe Elementary School at Park View were surprised Thursday morning by a sudden influx of federal agents and National Guard troops in the neighborhood, all assisted by a low-flying U.S. Park Police helicopter circling above.

“Some parents asked them what they were doing. They said they were being a friendly face and keeping the neighborhood safe and beautiful,” a parent told The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle.

The initiative was part of President Donald Trump’s D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force, which since August 2025 has used federal resources to more aggressively fight crime in the city. Authorities say declining crime numbers this year prove it’s working.

But critics say the deployment into residential neighborhoods like Park View — and around a school whose student body is predominantly Latino — is too much.

“They see these people and the vests and they think ICE. They are in a constant state of fear,” said one person.

“As a parent, I don’t want my kids to get used to armed guards patrolling the street,” added another.

Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau criticized the federal show of force. “It’s time for federal agents to leave our communities alone,” she said.

That’s not likely to happen anytime soon, though. Trump has pledged to keep the National Guard in D.C. until 2029, for one. But Janeese Lewis George, the Democratic nominee for mayor, has said she will more aggressively fight federal interference in the District and will immediately end cooperation between D.C. police and federal law enforcement agencies.





FROM THE COURTHOUSE

Questioning heated up Thursday in the bribery trial of Ward 8 council member Trayon White. Defense attorney Warren Gary Kohlman pressed FBI informant and star government witness Allieu Kamara on his trustworthiness and called his testimony “a performance.” Kamara struck back, repeatedly accusing Kohlman of putting words in his mouth.

Kohlman’s arguments took further shape: When asking Kamara about his meetings with White, which the FBI filmed because Kamara was secretly acting as an informant, Kohlman highlighted the parts of the video that made his client more sympathetic. White can be heard expressing hesitation about taking the money, and often looked distracted while Kamara discussed plans for future kickbacks.

Kamara, quick to dispute the defense at every turn, replied, “[White] put the money in his pocket and took it.”

Kohlman also attempted to frame exchanges of money as relatively commonplace — and not necessarily evidence of bribery — because of Kamara’s history of giving White generous campaign contributions in cash. And he raised questions about Kamara’s character, pressing him on billing issues with his D.C. government contracts and allegedly fraudulent tax returns.

Kamara testified that he indeed had a checkered past, committing fraud with pandemic loans and bribing several government officials. But he said he made an agreement with the U.S. government that he would tell the truth and cooperate with them, in exchange for the possibility of a lesser sentence for those crimes.

“If Trayon goes to jail, it doesn’t matter. If Trayon walks out of here, it doesn’t matter,” he said. “All I have to do is tell the truth.”






FROM THE DISTRICT

Trump’s proposed triumphal arch will negatively affect nearby historic sites. The National Park Service said it should be built anyway, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. The project, part of Trump’s campaign to reshape D.C., has faced legal pushback for its potential to obstruct the view of Arlington National Cemetery. WAMU reports that some are worried the arch’s proximity to DCA will further complicate an already crowded airspace.

D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser is in legacy-building mode. In a letter to the D.C. Council, Bowser said that in her final three months in office she would push forward with long-awaited development projects involving Chevy Chase, Poplar Point and the Frank D. Reeves Center on U Street. She’s also promising a bill to finance the renovation of Nationals Park to turn it into a "state-of-the-art venue that competes with newer facilities."

A federal judge ordered the Kennedy Center yesterday to provide a detailed update on its “temporary closure” and emergency repairs by Wednesday, but denied a request for an emergency hearing, The Sun’s Angie Orellana Hernandez and Torrie Herrington report. The order comes less than a day after new photos of Trump renewed fears that he plans to demolish the Kennedy Center as part of his bid to attach his name to the institution.

The Metro’s Yellow Line will be shut down over the next two weekends to work on the route’s rail infrastructure as part of WMATA’s new infrastructure program, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

A former youth minister for a Northern Virginia church faces federal child-exploitation charges after authorities said he sexually groomed multiple boys across the country under the guise of spiritual guidance, Covert reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Trump rescinded an Obama-era executive order on Wednesday that has long directed federal agencies’ restoration of the Chesapeake Bay, the Banner reports.





METRO MOMENT

Reddit DC cat (1470x1350, AR: 1.09)This week, a Redditor sought help to fetch a kitten stranded beneath an overpass in Navy Yard. After an hourslong effort involving the fire department, the SPCA and many good Samaritan civilians, he was saved. The Sun talked to the husband-wife team who finally got him down. (Responses have been lightly edited for length and clarity.)

What brought you onto the scene?

Danielle Joray: I volunteer with A Cat’s Life Rescue in PG County, I'm their trapping coordinator. There's a Facebook page called the DC Community Cat Club — it's a bunch of not only cat lovers but rescue people — and somebody had reposted the Reddit thread.

Andrew Marquesen: Danielle sent me the photo of the poor little cat sticking its head over the edge. I was working probably, like, a mile from there, and we were kind of having a slow day anyway. I was able to obtain a trap, got some cat food and headed down there.

What did it take to get the kitten down?

Marquesen: We couldn't see where it was. You could just hear it meowing. The Brandywine Valley SPCA showed up; we basically devised a plan to box the cat in by putting a trap on either side of that little ledge that the cat was on, just hoping he was hungry enough that he would not pass up the food. Maybe like 10 minutes later, the cat walked into the trap.

Where is he now?

Joray: He's at the BV SPCA. They named him London; he's going to get adopted. People were already offering to adopt him, which is awesome, but it's been a really slow time for all rescues in the area for adoptions.

Marquesen: This one was high-profile because it was in a busy area of town and up on an overpass, but as far as cat rescue stories go, this really wasn't that extraordinary of a story. There's a lot of cats that are rescued from similar perils that need to find homes as well.

Have an image from around D.C. you want to share? A question for our reporters? An “only in D.C.” moment? Tell us about it.




SPORTS

D991C51B-A1A2-4F56-BCAA-270DDB32923F copy 2.jpg (1458x972, AR: 1.50)The Goodman League is an institution in Southeast D.C. The long-running basketball league, played in Barry Farm, is a way for the community to connect, relax and enjoy some hoops. But Barry Farm, like so many D.C. neighborhoods, is quickly changing. And the league, approaching its 50th anniversary season next year, now faces an uncertain future. The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad talked to the league’s organizers and supporters about what it takes to keep a tradition alive.

By now, you may have seen the viral special teams play from Sunday’s Commanders game. It was made by Tyler Owens, a third-year safety. J.J. Watt, an NFL analyst and future Hall of Famer, called it “legitimately one of the greatest football plays I've ever seen.” But what was it like on the field? The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson talked to Owens, his teammates and his coaches to put together a moment-by-moment breakdown of a rep to remember.

Alex Ovechkin addressed his recent appearance in a pro-Putin ad, saying at Capitals training camp Thursday that he supports his home country of Russia and wants “peace and love for everybody,” The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports. When asked about the blowback Ovechkin has received, Caps GM Chris Patrick said, “I feel bad for him. … It may not be a popular sentiment among people critiquing him right now, but it’s a hard situation for him.”

entries.title: Working Hard or Hardly Working?
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Congress’ surprisingly good attendance record. An exclusive look at a DNC fundraising haul. Hegseth’s guy is probably not going to be Army secretary. Inside Democrats’ fight to change House seniority rules. And: Go west, data centers, to build on public lands.





THE LATEST

Surprise! Congress did something functional. Attendance has been impressive in both chambers, with members being present for about 97% of the votes this Congress, The Washington Sun’s data cruncher Andrew Van Dam shows us today with charts made from data assembled by Voteview. If these numbers hold — likely but not guaranteed, as attendance often falls during the holidays — it’ll be the second-best record ever, behind only the COVID-proxy-vote-assisted 2021-2022 cycle.

YAgdB-this-congress-had-excellent-attendance-.png (900x910, AR: 0.99)Speaker Mike Johnson has repeatedly called this “the most productive Congress in 80 years,” citing giant pieces of legislation snaked through the Capitol’s thin majorities through a combination of presidential threats and reconciliation rules.

Attendance was a big part of that. Leadership regularly needed as many members as they could scrounge up to pass bills with narrow margins. And they did it! Not that the public is all that grateful, mind you — polls show Americans still generally seem to think Congress is not doing much that they like.

Attendance is “the bane of any leader’s job,” former Harry Reid staffer Jim Manley told The Sun’s Manuela Silva. Manley said that in his time working for Reid, just as important as who showed up to floor votes was who showed up to committee meetings and votes. For example, the farm bill finally moved out of the Senate Agriculture Committee this week once Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) returned.

Who missed the most votes? Rep. Frederica Wilson (D-Florida) in the House and McConnell in the Senate. Both were born in 1942, and both have well-publicized health issues.

EfBtq-who-missed-the-most-votes-.png (900x846, AR: 1.06)More: Congress Hears an Apocalyptic Prediction From the ‘Godfather of AI’ • Federal Judges in Minnesota Speak Out Against Trump’s DOJ in Rare Interviews • Texas Democrat Sees a Fundraising Surge Following Opponent’s Racist Posts

Open tabs:

  • Inside the White House Tussle to Sway Trump on AI (WSJ)
  • States prep for ICE agents to be at polls, just in case (Axios)
  • Democrats keep pressure on Jeffries to punish rogue members (Politico)
  • How Trump’s New Green Card Policy Could Affect Immigrant Families (NYT)




FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


First on The Sun: Democratic donors are giving to the DNC again. The Democratic National Committee notched two of its highest grassroots fundraising months in a midterm cycle in years, bringing in more than a combined $14 million in July and August, The Sun’s Elena Schneider reports. The haul even surpassed the DNC’s total during the same period in 2018, when Democrats gained about 40 House seats.

Fundraising support from potential 2028ers helped, including Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Sens. Chris Murphy and Mark Kelly.

But this haul is merely a drop in the bucket. The DNC faces a massive funding gap with its chief rival, the Republican National Committee — not to mention Donald Trump’s own war chest, which has started to flood the zone with ads.

FROM THE HILL


It’s not looking good for Sean Parnell. Republican senators are pushing back on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s preferred choice for next Army secretary, The Sun’s Joe Gould reports. Parnell has been serving as a close adviser to Hegseth and is the Pentagon’s top spokesperson, but there’s not much interest on the Hill in giving him a promotion.

“It’s hard for me to imagine that could possibly happen,” Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota) said of Parnell’s chances of being confirmed if he’s nominated.

FROM A POTENTIAL FUTURE


Younger House Democrats make their move. “It’s an uphill battle, but I think the tide is turning,” a House Democrat working on a plan to wrest top committee slots from senior members next Congress told The Sun. Our Oriana González and Stephen Neukam go inside the effort to give younger, fresher faces a chance in the spotlight if the party wins control.

Term limits for a given member serving as either a committee chair or ranking member are an obvious solution, and one that the House Republican Conference has employed for years. But Democrats pushing for similar rules in their caucus are up against an entrenched seniority system backed by some older members and powerful groups like the Congressional Black Caucus.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

There are more data centers being considered for public lands than previously known. The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing proposals covering at least 17,600 acres of public land across six states: Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming, The Sun’s Mara Hoplamazian and Jade Lozada report. There are at least 12 data center projects under consideration, they write, and almost all the proposals appear to be in early stages. Last week we reported on the all-out effort to open up public lands to data center development.



More: Trump Administration Allows Inadvertent Killing of Endangered Species • DOJ Officials Brush Off a Judge’s Contempt Warning in the Epstein Files Case • Josh Shapiro Calls for Federal Government to Place ‘Strict Guardrails’ on AI 





NOT US

  • Mansions, Jets, and the Secret White House Watch: The New Status Symbols of Trump’s Washington, by Aidan McLaughlin for Vanity Fair
  • Trump emphasizes crime in midterm push in North Carolina, by Isaac Arnsdorf, Katherine Doyle and Cleve R. Wootson Jr. for The Washington Post

entries.title: Trump Is Considering More Data Centers on Public Lands Than Previously Known
entries.summary: The data center proposals cover at least 17,600 acres of public lands across six Western states.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is considering proposals for at least 12 data centers and data center-related infrastructure projects to be built on federal public lands — far more than previously known.

The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing data center-related proposals covering at least 17,600 acres of public land across six states — Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming, according to public records of right-of-way proposals reviewed by The Washington Sun.

Many of the projects under consideration haven’t been previously reported, and aren’t easily accessible on BLM’s website. Several local officials told The Sun they weren’t aware of the federal government’s deliberations, prompting transparency concerns among community advocates.

“If there are places where communities think it is appropriate to build data centers, focus on those,” said Aaron Weiss, director of the conservation group Center for Western Priorities. “The Trump administration needs to stop cutting the public out of public land management. The solution is more public notice and more opportunities for stakeholders to shape projects on the front end.”

Building data centers on public lands, as well as supporting infrastructure like access roads and water pipelines, has emerged as a priority for the Trump administration, which directed BLM officials to identify lands that could be suitable. The administration has pushed to accelerate data center infrastructure development despite public backlash and mounting fears around artificial intelligence.

Public lands in the U.S. are required to be managed for multiple uses, which have historically included mining, logging, energy production and livestock grazing. Building data centers on public lands is unprecedented, however.

Some of the proposals are for projects under development on a mix of private and public lands that have approvals from local officials. But local officials and advocates in Utah, Arizona, Oregon, Idaho and Wyoming told The Sun they weren’t aware of many of the projects.

In Utah, a nuclear energy startup appears to be proposing two data centers powered by small nuclear reactors. In Arizona, BLM is considering four proposals for data center-related infrastructure that could collectively use more than 3,000 acres of public land.

Almost all of the proposals appear to be in early stages. A BLM spokesperson said each proposal will be evaluated under the National Environmental Policy Act process to ensure potential environmental impacts are “understood, disclosed and appropriately addressed.”

“This process helps protect natural resources while enabling responsible infrastructure development that can deliver benefits to the American people, such as expanded broadband capacity, improved electrical reliability, and support for growing technology-driven economies,” the spokesperson said.

The NEPA process includes public notice and a comment period, though the Trump administration has rolled back NEPA regulations and narrowed opportunities for public input.

Exact locations for the projects, as well as the scope and size of each project, will be publicly available once the NEPA process is underway. So far, only one data center on public land has been approved, and that project, in Nevada, is on hold following a legal challenge.

While some projects involve building full data centers on public lands, others would involve only infrastructure to support data centers. In Wyoming, Prometheus Hyperscale has submitted proposals for rights-of-way for an access road, telecommunications line and water pipeline on public lands.

The largest proposal appears to be a 10,200-acre project from Valar Atomics, a nuclear power start-up that has received support from the Department of Energy for their efforts to quickly develop technology for small nuclear reactors.

That company is proposing a data center co-located with small nuclear reactors at a site near Green River, Utah. Valar Atomics has a second proposal for another data center combined with nuclear reactors in Utah called the “Raceway Gigasite,” which doesn’t currently have an estimated size.

Valar Atomics has publicly announced a smaller project with Nvidia that they say will show off technology meant to conserve water.

Valar Atomics did not respond to a request for comment.

There is little public awareness of those projects in Utah, said Lexi Tuddenham, executive director of HEAL Utah, an environmental advocacy group.

“It’s really, really hard to find information about this stuff, and I think it’s representative of the way the industry in general is operating with a lack of transparency that I think is really deeply concerning,” she said. “Both the AI industry and the nuclear industry, which seem to be in this unholy alliance right now.”

Other proposals include four data center-related infrastructure projects in Arizona, one data center in Idaho, at least three in Nevada and one in Oregon. At least four projects are proposed by Copia Power, a developer that has historically worked on renewable energy projects. Copia withdrew a proposal for another data center in Wyoming this summer.

Copia declined to comment for this story.

In Idaho, Rhea Data, a subsidiary of Nevada-based Arevia Power, proposed a 4,000,000-square-foot multi-building data center on 3,226 acres of public lands a few miles south of Boise, according to a BLM spokesperson. The development would include a natural gas power generation facility and electrical facilities to connect to the Idaho Power Company, a local utility.

That project is also connected to a sprawling utility-scale solar energy project proposed by another subsidiary of Arevia Power, which is also seeking a right-of-way on public lands, according to BLM.

The data center projects raise concerns among environmental advocates that new data centers will increase energy rates for locals, and that the data centers and nonrenewable energy sources that could power them will intensify pollution.

“If there were to be more [data centers], I honestly don’t know what that would even look like,” said Lisa Young, director of the Sierra Club’s Idaho chapter. “Would that mean even more gas plants? Would that mean turning back on coal plants longer? What does that mean for our water resources? It’s honestly kind of apocalyptic to think about.”

Arevia Power did not respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

In Oregon, BLM is considering a right-of-way application from Copia Power for a data center on public lands. Data centers are no stranger to Oregon, where 142 centers are operating or planned, according to an April Pew Research Center study.

But Ben Brint, the senior climate program director at the Oregon Environmental Council, had never heard of using federal public lands to build one.

“In Oregon, this would be a really bad precedent,” Brint said. “Some very large percentage of the state is public lands, and if we’re starting to allow that, that’s large swaths of the state that really could be at risk of further development.”

entries.title: The DNC Gets a Fundraising Boost After Months of Struggle
entries.summary: The Democratic National Committee had a big summer with grassroots donors, taking some of the edge off a difficult year.
entries.content:
The Democratic National Committee racked up two of its biggest grassroots fundraising months in a midterm cycle this summer, bringing in more than $14 million combined in July and August.

The grassroots totals surpassed what the DNC hit in those two months in 2018, the midterm cycle during President Donald Trump’s first term, according to data the committee shared first with The Washington Sun. The committee also hit 1 million unique individual donors for the cycle this summer, a traditionally sleepy time for fundraising.

The surge got some help from several potential 2028 presidential candidates who lent their fundraising muscle to the party committee’s efforts, a DNC official said, including Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy. Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, another potential 2028 candidate, helped to raise $640,000 through a contest to win a trip to Washington, D.C., and tour the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum with him.

But the DNC’s strength with small-dollar donors doesn’t close the gaping hole in the party committee’s bank account, especially when compared to the Republican National Committee. As of July, the DNC had $16 million in cash on hand, but $18 million in debts. The RNC ended July with more than $130 million in cash.

Both committees will file their full financial fundraising disclosures for August with the Federal Election Commission on Sunday.

The DNC has faced months of bad headlines, including its financial woes and its botched 2024 election autopsy. DNC Chair Ken Martin, who has endured a rocky tenure atop the committee, indicated to allies last month he was open to overhauling how the DNC raised money, including bringing in more fundraising talent.

“I’d rather not be in the red, but if you look at ActBlue versus WinRed totals, you wouldn’t come away thinking Democrats are underfunded,” said Kenneth Pennington, a Democratic digital fundraising consultant, referring to the small-dollar donation platforms affiliated with the Democratic and Republican Party respectively. “When you look at the spending advantages on the hard side that Democrats have, they’re sizable. Where we’re falling behind is on some of the soft side stuff, party support stuff, that has historically been driven by big donors.”

Pennington also said that the DNC’s grassroots fundraising is a sign of voter enthusiasm that will translate into votes come November, just as it did in 2018. That confidence is born out in public and private polling, where Democrats regularly hold an intensity advantage. Republicans are anxiously eying Democrats’ voter turnout surge throughout the 2026 primary season as another indicator for that enthusiasm edge.

“I’m feeling good about our party’s base, that’s motivated, donating $20 by huge numbers of people, rather than the party that’s raising money by Elon Musk cutting one check,” he added.

So far, the DNC has raised nearly $16 million more from small-dollar donors at this point in the cycle than it did in 2018, $52.3 million to $36.6 million, when Democrats netted 40 congressional seats.

“While Republicans rely on billionaire donors to try and bail them out from their unpopular policies and tanking approval ratings, Democrats are powered by grassroots donors,” Martin said in a statement shared with The Sun. “It’s clear they are fired up heading into the midterms.”
entries.author: Elena Schneider

entries.title: In D.C.’s Barry Farm, Basketball Is Played Against a Changing Backdrop
entries.summary: The long-running Goodman League, a summer tradition in Southeast Washington, faces an uncertain future.
entries.content:
As afternoon turned to evening on a warm Sunday in early September, vendors started setting up around the Barry Farm Recreation Center in Southeast D.C. They unpacked bottles of top-shelf liquor and mixers. They erected tents to sell soul food, jollof rice and Caribbean plates. One covered a table with shea butter, holistic remedies and a book of D.C. slang.

A short time later, people from around the District started to pass by, making their way to the final game of the year for the Goodman League, a long-running outdoor basketball league that has become an iconic summer tradition in this part of the city. They had come to watch basketball but also to connect and celebrate, many of them former residents of the Barry Farm area.

The bleachers filled well before tipoff of that night’s game, a championship meeting between the fan-favorite Street Athletes against the World Class Ballers. The pregame soundtrack featured exclusively go-go as fans hugged friends and sparked up hazy, herbal clouds. One woman started circulating with homemade drinks she called “ring-a-lings.” Not far from the court, one couple set up a playpen for their toddler, who peered out at the action.

Parking started to get scarce, and many drivers resorted to double-parking or pulling up on sidewalks. Miles Rawls, the league’s commissioner and de facto commentator, grabbed the mic and warned about potential towing.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“Whoever has that Porsche down at the bottom, tend to your vehicle,” he announced to the growing crowd.

Rawls took over as commissioner in 1996, nearly 20 years after the league was founded. The court, widely referred to as the “Barry Farm coliseum,” was once next to the Barry Farm Dwellings, a sprawling, 400-unit public housing complex built in the 1940s. But those buildings were demolished in 2019 as part of the New Communities Initiative created under Mayor Muriel Bowser. Now, the coliseum sits in the shadow of two new apartment buildings — tangible proof that Barry Farm, like so many neighborhoods in the city, is changing.

This championship game marked the final contest of the 2026 season, with a murky future ahead. Although Rawls has already spent time plotting his institution’s 50th anniversary next summer, he’s unsure how the league will fit into the neighborhood. But there will be plenty of colder months to worry about that — ahead of the championship game, with a mic in his hand, he had nothing but pride.

“World Class Ballers … Street Athletes … live from the coliseum [in] Southeast D.C. where I was what?!” he asked the crowd.

“Born and raised!” they responded

Bittersweet


Detrice Belt, the president of the Barry Farm Tenants and Allies Association, attended the first game of the Goodman season in May, and that was enough.

“It's very bittersweet,” she said. “It's bittersweet because you see some faces that you haven't seen, and then you don't see a lot of faces because people can't get there. [Others] have died.”

Belt remembers what the summer league was like before. Neighbors would walk to the games and go home for food. Everyone knew where the candy lady was located. Parking wasn’t necessary but if it got crowded, nobody worried about a tow. But the neighborhood is different now. The townhomes that loomed over the basketball court are gone. So is the corner store. So is the candy lady.

Belt has left, too. Despite her position in the tenants association, she no longer lives in Barry Farm. In 2019, Belt was one of the last residents to leave the Dwellings. She gave her two pit bulls to family and accepted the city's help in moving herself, her daughter and her nearly 30-year-old turtle into a new building in Northeast D.C. The city continues to pay for the storage of some of her belongings and has offered her a spot at one of the neighborhood’s new apartment buildings. But Belt said she’s waiting for a townhome, like the one she had before. Besides, she’s not sure what the neighborhood will look like in a few years.

“A lot of people don't want to return,” she said. “Because it was such a nightmare of being pushed out. So you don't know if you're going to get pushed out again by these new people, by the homeowners, by the new rules of the developers, because the rules will change.”

The new community is being developed through a public-private partnership between the D.C. Housing Authority and the Preservation of Affordable Housing, a nonprofit. It will be a mix of rentals, private homes and affordable housing.

goodman_league.jpg (8091x6000, AR: 1.35)
Maia Shanklin Roberts, a vice president of real estate development for POAH, emphasized that the redevelopment is focused on safeguarding institutions like the Goodman League.

“You can't ignore the trauma of the relocation and the demolition of the buildings,” she said. “Everything that we do is about restoring and repairing the relationship between community and the project, because we now have to build a new relationship.”

Roberts said she’s confident that providing the community more amenities will help rebuild trust: a grocery store, a community center, discounted rent on brick-and-mortar sites for Ward 8 businesses. But it’s also clear that the new Barry Farm will probably be made up of people unaware of the area’s history or traditions.

“[The Goodman League] is an institution, but we also have new residents and new people that live in Ward 8 and Anacostia and the surrounding community who want to be a part of the project,” Roberts said.

She admits that developers did not factor the league or its impact into the original plans. She has developed a relationship with Rawls, even raising the idea of moving the league to another location within the community. But those talks have not been fruitful.

“What I have now accepted as developer is that it is going to be there, and so what we need to do is create a place,” Roberts said.

Now, Roberts’ team is working with landscape designers to create better lighting and amenities around the current court. She’s not sure if parking will ever improve.

‘I Wanna Thank You’


By the game’s third quarter, it became clear that the World Class Ballers were going to win the Goodman League title. As the team built its lead, children took over the court with every timeout, taking their own shots in front of the crowd. Even as the score grew lopsided, Rawls tried to keep his commentary light.

“Put him on spin cycle, extra heavy, tumble, no dryer sheets!” he screamed after a highlight play.

Rawls, who considers himself to be a “day-by-day type of guy,” said he’s not planning to worry about next summer until the spring. But the end of this season had made him wistful.

“Throughout the week and all of that, that's when it’ll really hit me,” he said. “It's been a spectacular week, a spectacular season and a great 30 years.”

It was after 11 p.m. when the game ended. Final score: World Class Ballers 80, Street Athletes 73. A few fans, upset about the local Street Athletes team going down, hurled bottles onto the court. Ring-a-lings flew through the air. Rawls got on the mic, warning them to stop.

“Whoever it is, if you hit the wrong motherfucker, it's gonna be a problem,” he said. “It's a good motherfucking game. Great season. Don't do that bama shit.”

As the debris continued raining down, he issued the threat he reserves for when he is most upset.

“Somebody hit me with something, I'm telling you right fucking now — when I move my shit indoors next year, y'all gone wonder why,” he said.

Eventually, the commotion died down and a more laid-back, cookout vibe took over. Maze and Frankie Beverly’s “I Wanna Thank You” played over speakers as fans hugged goodbye. Wayne Hall, the father who set up the playpen, started packing it away. He played in the league until 2002, and said it was a blessing to be able to still come to the Goodman games with his toddler, who watches from “his own space.”

Hall’s partner, Northeast native Lyndsay Briscoe, said she has been coming to the games for at least 16 years. Now that she has two young children, she loves being able to include them in what she sees as a quintessentially D.C. tradition. She said people have long questioned the viability of the Goodman League in a changing D.C., but she’s hoping her son will have a chance to follow in his father’s footsteps.

“Like, ‘Hey, Mom, I want to have something to do after camp,’” she imagined her son saying. “‘I want to go down to the Goodman League and play with my friends.’”

As a go-go version of “I Wanna Thank You” played over the speakers and the last visitors headed to their cars, Rawls took a second to consider the future of the league, the neighborhood and all of the fans who had just left his basketball court.

“If the neighborhood is still Barry Farm, they’re coming for the Goodman League,” he said. “That's what they're here for. When you build a good product, the people are going to follow you, no matter where you go.”
